Text: Horse-like. No-one, even devotees of the saddle, would be likely to buy a perfume smelling of horses, yet this note is not unknown in perfumery, as just a touch of artistry where appropriate as, for example, in leather compositions. A few aroma chemicals in regular use smell of horse urine which, quite unfairly, might be taken to confirm the most vociferous proclamations of those who delight in condemning the occasional fleeting suggestion of malodour emanating from a local perfume factory. Some para-cresyl esters, the acetate for example, are offensively horsey only in high concentration, and give usefully pleasing notes of the Narcissus type when suitably diluted and blended.

Text: This is a term of malodour, referring to the odour of waste matter from the bowel, the relationship of which to perfumery would appear to be remote. However, Civet, as we have mentioned, possesses much of this type of odour, and it is observed also in the aroma chemicals indole and skatole, both found in human faeces, the first-named of which occurs as a natural constituent of the absolutes of Jasmin and Orange Flower. In his interesting and illuminating book, 'The Practice of Modern Perfumery,' Paul Jellinek puts forward a thought- provoking theory of the psychological effects of odours, including animalic odours, as components of the fragrance profiles of perfumes.
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 3 odour vocabulary, PDF p.71

Text: The element sulphur is odourless, and so, strictly speaking, there should be no such experience as a 'sulphurous' odour. But to speak strictly in reference to some odours is to fall into all sorts of trouble, and it is a fact that the term 'sulphurous', or simply 'sulphur', in reference to the odours of certain compounds of sulphur, has been used for centuries. The accepted meaning of 'sulphurous' is well exemplified by the odour of the gas hydrogen sulphide, which smells of rotten eggs (because eggs in a rotten condition give off the gas), and by sulphur dioxide, the odour of which is unusual, giving a distinct flavour impression before we perceive anything approaching a frue odour of the gas. A coke brazier gives rise to this effect from the oxidation of metal sulphides, and if inhaled downwind the sulphur dioxide constricts the air passages of the lungs in a most unpleasant way. On approaching the fire a stinging sensation in the nose may be observed; this is caused by stimulation of endings of the trigeminal nerves, presumably by oxonium ions from the ionisation of sulphurous acid. Some equations will make this clear: (i) Sulphur dioxide is produced by atmospheric oxidation of metal sulphides (MS, say) present as impurities in coke at the high temperature of the brazier: 2MS (ii) The sulphur dioxide reacts with moisture in the air or in the nose to form sulphurous acid. The above reaction occurs wherever sulphur dioxide encounters moisture, as it does when inhaled. Hence the true odour effect (and 'flavour') of the gas may not be that of the gas itself, but of sulphurous acid, or just possibly free hydrogen sulphite or sulphite ions—see (iii), below. Text: Tropical flowers display a very wide range of odours. Among many of their fragrances, however, there is some common factor of intense, narcotic sweetness, diffusiveness of odour and unique floral character which in the absence of adequate words may be likened to the trumpet lily fragrance—but far, far sweeter and more powerful. Examples abound, but are perhaps typified by Plumeria, Gardenia and White Ginger. This kind of fragrance, together with that of the typical surrounding greenery, might be regarded as deserving of a descriptor of its own, and we offer the word 'tropical' as a possible candidate.
